content: 1. Poison information centers provide specialized advice on diagnosing and managing poisoning cases across all age groups, exposure routes, and circumstances, including accidental, intentional, occupational, or environmental exposures. 2. These centers handle a wide range of toxic agents, including consumer products, pharmaceuticals, substances of abuse, environmental chemicals, natural toxins, pesticides, and industrial chemicals. 3. They play a critical role in poisoning prevention strategies, public outreach, response to chemical incidents, training, and public health toxicovigilance. 4. Poison information centers promote cost-effective, evidence-based management of poisoning cases, avoiding unnecessary or ineffective treatments. 5. These centers serve healthcare professionals and, in many countries, the general public. Other users include government bodies, emergency services, regulatory agencies, public health services, academia, and industry. 6. Poison information centers are typically staffed by specialists trained in toxicology, who provide timely and accurate information on toxicological issues, including product composition, clinical features of exposure, toxicity likelihood and severity, treatment requirements, and clinical management. 7. To function effectively, these centers require access to extensive toxicological and product databases and should ideally be supported by physicians trained in clinical toxicology for complex or severe cases. 8. Poison information centers must operate independently and impartially to provide authoritative services without conflicts of interest. 9. Confidentiality and data storage practices must comply with national legal, clinical, and ethical standards. 10. Government recognition of poison information centers is essential to ensure their sustainability and formalize their roles and responsibilities, particularly in toxicovigilance. 11. Most poison information centers are located within healthcare facilities, such as hospitals, to ensure access to emergency and intensive care services and a network of medical disciplines. 12. Centers located in teaching institutions, such as medical schools or universities, benefit from access to libraries, research facilities, and educational activities. 13. Centers based in public health institutes or ministries can focus more on poisoning prevention and maintain closer relationships with decision-making authorities. 14. Poison information centers should ideally operate 24/7 and have dedicated, secure facilities for their operations and information storage. 15. Staff at poison information centers may include physicians, nurses, scientists (e.g., biochemists, biologists, chemists), pharmacists, or a combination of these professionals. 16. Key staff roles include the director, administrative and operations manager, specialists in poison information, medical toxicologists, and support staff. 17. A fully operational center providing 24-hour service requires at least one medical toxicologist and adequate staffing to handle inquiries and provide medical advice.
